title: COP31 negotiators race toward a climate compromise after overtime
lead: After the scheduled deadline passed, diplomats in Antalya tried to rescue a global climate agreement that could satisfy countries with very different energy priorities.
body: The COP31 summit did not end neatly when its official timetable expired. Negotiators from nearly 200 countries continued their conversations as a revised draft took shape, with host Turkey and lead negotiator Australia working together to find language that delegations could accept.

The toughest questions remained how explicitly to address fossil fuels and how to finance adaptation for vulnerable economies. The late-night text suggested a possible landing zone, but its publication did not itself mean that every country had approved the outcome.
why: The wording of a climate agreement matters because countries use it to judge future investment, energy policy and financial support.

title: A COP31 draft reignites the fight over fossil fuels
lead: A draft published near the end of the UN summit drew attention for what it left unsaid about the fuels driving global warming.
body: Turkey's summit presidency circulated late-stage wording that critics believed did not adequately address fossil-fuel use. The dispute revealed how differently governments interpret responsibility for cutting emissions while meeting current energy needs.

Environmental advocates wanted unmistakable language about moving away from oil, gas and coal. Others stressed economic transition, national circumstances and the need for financing, leaving negotiators with the difficult task of reaching consensus.
why: Debates over a few paragraphs can shape how governments understand the direction of international climate commitments.

title: Why China is cautious about becoming the world's climate leader
lead: China's industrial reach and clean-energy manufacturing make it pivotal to climate policy, but Beijing has reasons to avoid assuming the full diplomatic burden.
body: Analysis published during the Antalya summit examined the difference between China's capacity to influence energy transitions and its willingness to take the leading international role. Economic priorities, development arguments and geopolitical expectations all complicate that calculation.
The question is not simply whether China builds renewable technology. It is whether the country is prepared to accept the political and financial expectations that international leadership may carry.
why: The world's emissions trajectory depends on cooperation among major economies, even when no single nation wants to lead alone.

title: Europe's plastic-waste export ban brings a new recycling challenge
lead: The European Union's restrictions on shipping plastic waste to countries outside the OECD entered a new phase, forcing attention back to domestic recycling capacity.
body: Sending discarded plastic overseas has long allowed wealthier markets to move the burden of processing waste elsewhere. The EU rule is intended to reduce that practice for destinations outside the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development.

The change places a spotlight on how plastic is collected, sorted, reused and recycled within Europe. The environmental benefit will depend not only on the regulation but on the infrastructure and enforcement behind it.
why: Waste policy is increasingly linked to manufacturing, trade and environmental justice across borders.

title: Students across Europe turn education and climate frustrations into protests
lead: Young demonstrators organized actions across dozens of European countries, bringing a wide set of concerns into the streets.
body: Organizers described coordinated protests across 25 European nations. The campaigns did not all make the same demand: issues ranged from funding for schools to climate action and questions about young people's role in public decisions.

That diversity matters. The demonstrations were less a single-issue movement than a sign that a generation wants to influence choices affecting classrooms, living standards and the future environment.
why: Youth participation can change what governments and institutions regard as urgent issues.

title: US governors and lawmakers keep a climate presence at COP31
lead: Although Washington did not send an official delegation, American state and local figures appeared in force at the UN climate conference.
body: Democratic lawmakers, governors, former officials and municipal leaders joined discussions in Antalya following their party's election gains. A coalition called America Is All In brought a delegation that rivaled or exceeded the size of many countries' official teams.

Participants argued that state and city policy still matters even when federal climate priorities change. Their presence highlighted the unusual fact that climate diplomacy can involve many layers of government at once.
why: National policy is important, but local governments often control decisions about transport, buildings and electricity demand.

title: Climate summit renews debate over making polluters finance adaptation
lead: Civil-society groups and international voices called for stronger ways to make high-emitting industries contribute toward climate-related costs.
body: At COP31 in Antalya, the idea of asking fossil-fuel polluters to pay more toward climate action gained renewed attention. Advocates argued that the financial consequences of rising temperatures should not fall primarily on countries and communities with the fewest resources.
The debate was not about one universally agreed tax formula. It was about who should finance adaptation and how the cost of emissions could be reflected more directly in public policy.
why: Climate adaptation involves real spending on resilience, infrastructure and protection from increasingly costly weather events.

title: Trump, Xi and Putin issue a declaration after an unusual summit
lead: A high-profile meeting involving the leaders of the United States, China and Russia produced a public peace declaration and intense diplomatic scrutiny.
body: The three-way meeting at an Asia-Pacific summit in Shenzhen was unusual because leaders from governments with deep disagreements appeared together to discuss global security and diplomacy. The resulting declaration was politically striking, though a joint statement is not the same thing as a solved conflict.

The gathering raised fresh questions about the influence of large powers and what smaller countries can expect from talks held at the highest level. Its consequences will depend on concrete actions after the cameras leave.
why: Diplomatic breakthroughs must be judged by implementation, not only by the symbolism of leaders meeting.

title: Zelenskyy voices doubts about Moscow's readiness to compromise
lead: Ukraine's president responded cautiously to diplomatic signals following the latest talks involving Washington and Moscow.
body: Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he remained more skeptical than US officials about whether Vladimir Putin was prepared to make compromises. He also described remarks Donald Trump had made to European allies about the financial burden of the war.

The comments underline an enduring problem in peace diplomacy: participants can agree that talks are desirable without agreeing on the conditions for ending a conflict. Ukraine continues to argue that its own sovereignty and security must guide any outcome.
why: The credibility of proposed peace terms depends on whether the countries directly affected can accept and implement them.

title: Japan's prime minister raises difficult issues with Putin at APEC
lead: Tokyo confirmed talks on the sidelines of an international summit despite strained relations with Moscow.
body: Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi met Vladimir Putin during the APEC gathering in China, according to Japan's government. The discussion touched on the detention of a Japanese national in Russia and the treatment of Japanese business interests.
Officials said channels of communication would remain open. The exchange showed how neighboring countries can maintain diplomatic contact even when major disputes remain unresolved.
why: Regular communication can prevent misunderstandings without requiring governments to abandon their disagreements.
